answer:
HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded): Among NLSY79 respondents aged 24–32, older respondents are less likely to have taken more money out of savings than they put in. In the primary contrast (dissavers vs net savers), each additional year of age is associated with roughly 9% lower odds of dissaving (adjusted OR 0.915, 95% CI 0.896–0.934, p<0.001; unadjusted OR 0.891, 95% CI 0.874–0.909), with the adjusted predicted withdrawal probability falling from ~46% at age 24 to ~29% at age 32 (covariates held at sample means). The gradient is essentially linear: the centered AGE² term is statistically significant but tiny (OR 0.985, p=0.003), adding negligible curvature over a 24–32 age window.

IMPORTANT CAVEAT (mandatory sensitivity check): a large share of this apparent age gradient is a missing-data artifact. 3,963 rows (31.2%) have INCOME exactly equal to the sample mean (mean-imputed; 2,200 of them also carry the modal BMI value, i.e., heavily imputed records). The imputed share rises steeply with age (27% at ages 24–25 → 45% at age 32), and imputed rows have a much lower withdrawal rate (11.2% vs 29.2%). When these rows are excluded, the age effect disappears entirely — adjusted OR 0.999 (95% CI 0.974–1.024, p=0.93; unadjusted OR 0.987, p=0.28), with withdrawal rates flat at ~48–54% across ages 24–32. Adding an imputation flag as a control (full sample) weakens but does not eliminate the gradient (OR 0.968, p<0.001). Honest reading: the cross-sectional association "older → less likely to dissave" is present in the full data and robust to BMI winsorization and comparison-group definition, but it is largely compositional, driven by age-related income missingness; within the cleanest (observed-income) subsample there is no reliable age effect over 24–32. Any causal life-cycle claim is unwarranted from these cross-sectional data.

payload.hypothesis: Older respondents are less likely to withdraw more from savings than they put in: each additional year of age (24-32) is associated with ~9% lower odds of dissaving (adjusted OR 0.915, 95% CI 0.896-0.934, p<0.001; unadjusted OR 0.891), with adjusted predicted withdrawal probability falling from ~46% at age 24 to ~29% at age 32. The relationship is essentially linear (centered AGE^2 OR 0.985, p=0.003 - statistically significant but negligible curvature). Critical caveat: 31.2% of rows have mean-imputed income (their share rises from 27% at age 24 to 45% at age 32, and they withdraw far less often: 11.2% vs 29.2%), so the gradient is largely compositional; among respondents with observed income the age effect vanishes (adjusted OR 0.999, p=0.93; unadjusted OR 0.987, p=0.28; withdrawal rates flat at ~48-54%). The cross-sectional negative age gradient is therefore best read as 'older respondents dissave less', robust to covariate adjustment and comparison-group definition, but substantially attributable to age-related income missingness rather than a clean aging effect.
payload.workflow: 1) Inspection: 12,686 rows x 9 columns, no missing values; AGE 24-32; AGE_2 == AGE^2 exactly; DISSAVED x SAMESAVE crosstab confirmed three mutually exclusive savings categories with a residual net-saver group (DISSAVED=0 & SAMESAVE=0, n=4,913). 2) Primary contrast: dissavers (n=2,988) vs net savers (n=4,913), excluding the no-change/no-savings group (n=4,785). 3) Logistic regressions: unadjusted AGE-only; adjusted with log(INCOME+1), FEMALE, BLACK, HISPANIC, BMI; centered-AGE^2 quadratic; full-sample robustness; sensitivity excluding mean-imputed incomes; BMI winsorized at 1st/99th percentiles; imputation-flag control. 4) Imputation-artifact diagnostics (imputation rate by age, DISSAVED by imputed status, unadjusted model on observed-income rows). 5) Descriptives: single-year and 2-year banded withdrawal rates with n, exported as SVG bar charts. Outputs: output/model_table.csv, output/M2_full_coefficients.csv, output/age_banded_withdrawal_rates.svg, output/age_band_withdrawal_rates_2yr.svg, output/age_band_rates.csv.
